newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy trade minister sees no EMU threat from Buba.
newsitem.headline: Italy trade minister sees no EMU threat from Buba.

text.p: The German government's decision to revalue gold reserves in the face of Bundesbank criticism need not threaten the launch of a single European currency, Italy's Foreign Trade Minister Augusto Fantozzi said on Thursday.
Asked if the row between the German government and its central bank could put European Monetary Union in doubt, Fantozzi said "I don't think so and I hope not."
Fantozzi told Reuters Financial Television in an interview that he believed the Maastricht Treaty's strict criteria for EMU membership could be interpreted more flexibly.
"All concerned countries will probably be more reasonable and this, in my opinion, will make the starting of EMU easier," he said.

Germany, France and Italy are all struggling to meet one of the key criteria spelt out in the Maastricht Treaty -- a requirement to lower the public deficit to gross domestic product ratio to three percent by the end of 1997.

"The (Maastricht) parameters are part of the agreement and they have to be respected but you need a certain margin of flexibility and we have to adapt and use that flexibility," he added. Fantozzi was critical of Germany's gold revaluation plan, saying Italy would not be allowed to follow suit.

"I think revaluing the gold reserves has been judged by all concerned parties as a not correct approach," he said, adding "The Bank of Italy would not accept it and I think the European institutions ... would not accept it."

Italy had to stick to its chosen course of cutting back on state spending. "What we have to do is to take substantial concrete structural measures so we do not make the same mistake and it would make Italian participation easier."
Fantozzi said it would not be a disaster for Italy if it failed to qualify for the first wave of EMU, planned for launch in 1999.

"It will allow us to do things better ... if we have more time ... we will have less sacrifices for Italian citizens," he said. But he added: "We will play our game, as (like) the other countries, to be there from the very beginning." Rome newsroom +396-6782505
